    Track 0 · Foundations · Lesson 8

    How language models work: next-token prediction

    After this lesson you can trace a prompt all the way to generated text: how the model produces a probability for every next token, how it picks one, and how decoding settings like temperature change the output.

    Level: beginner Read time: ~10 min Prerequisites: Attention & the Transformer Updated: 13 Nov 2026

    We've assembled the machine: text becomes tokens, tokens become embeddings, and a stack of Transformer blocks gives every token a context-aware representation. This lesson connects that final representation to the one thing a language model is trained to do — predict the next token — and shows how repeating that prediction produces paragraphs.

    From the last layer to a guess about the next token

    After the Transformer stack, the representation at the last position is fed into a final linear layer called the LM head. It outputs one number for every token in the vocabulary — these raw scores are called logits. A high logit means "this token is a good continuation"; a low one means "unlikely."

    When you generate text, only the last position's prediction is used. During training the head runs at every position at once: position 1 predicts token 2, position 2 predicts token 3, and so on, all in one forward pass. The causal mask from Lesson 0.5 keeps each position from seeing its own answer. That is why a single forward pass over a 500-token example yields 499 next-token predictions, and 499 terms in the loss.

    Logits aren't probabilities (they can be negative, and they don't sum to 1). To convert them, the model applies softmax: exponentiate each logit and normalize so they're all positive and sum to 1. The result is a probability distribution over the next token — the model's full answer to "what comes next?"

    How it learns to do this: the training objective

    Pretraining is exactly the loop from Lesson 0.2, with one specific loss. Take an ocean of text, and at every position ask the model to predict the next token. The loss — cross-entropy — is large when the model assigned low probability to the token that actually came next, and small when it assigned high probability. Gradient descent then nudges the parameters to make the real next token more likely.

    The loss for one position is −ln p, where p is the probability the model gave the token that actually came next. It is measured in nats (natural-log units). With the distribution in the figure, if the true next token is "Paris" (p = 0.78) the loss is −ln 0.78 ≈ 0.25 nats. If the text had actually continued with "London" (p = 0.01), the loss is −ln 0.01 ≈ 4.6 nats. A model that spread probability evenly over SmolLM2's 49,152 tokens would score ln 49,152 ≈ 10.8 nats on every token, which is roughly where an untrained model starts. The training loss you will watch in Track 1 is this number averaged over every predicted token.

    The profound part: to get good at this one narrow game across trillions of tokens, the model is forced to internalize grammar, facts, styles, and reasoning patterns — because all of those help predict what comes next. "Just predicting the next token" is deceptively powerful. (We'll meet cross-entropy properly in Track 1; for now, "make the true next token more probable" is enough.)

    Key idea

    A base language model is a next-token probability machine. Everything it appears to "do" — answer, summarize, translate — is that machine producing one plausible token after another.

    Generation: do it again, and again

    One forward pass gives the distribution for a single next token. To produce more than one token, the model is autoregressive: it picks a next token, appends it to the sequence, and runs again to get the following token's distribution — repeating until it emits an end-of-sequence token or hits a length limit.

    tokens = tokenize(prompt)

    while not done:

      logits = model(tokens) # scores for next token

      probs = softmax(logits)

      next_tok = choose(probs) # see "decoding" below

      tokens.append(next_tok)

    Decoding: how a token is chosen

    That choose step is decoding, and it has settings you'll tune:

    • Greedy: always take the single most probable token (argmax). Deterministic and safe, but can be repetitive and bland.
    • Sampling: randomly draw a token according to the probabilities — more varied, more creative, occasionally wrong.
    • Temperature: a knob that sharpens or flattens the distribution before sampling. It divides the logits before the softmax, softmax(logits / T). Low temperature (→0) approaches greedy and stays "safe"; high temperature spreads probability out and increases surprise. More variety is not more accuracy.
    • Top-k: only sample from the k most probable tokens (e.g., 50) and renormalise (Fan et al. 2018, arXiv 1805.04833). Simple, but a fixed k is too many when the model is sure and too few when it isn't.
    • Top-p (nucleus): only sample from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p (e.g., 0.9), discarding the long tail of unlikely tokens (Holtzman et al. 2019, arXiv 1904.09751). Curbs nonsense while keeping variety.
    • Min-p: keep only tokens whose probability is at least a fraction of the top token's (e.g., min_p = 0.05 keeps tokens with at least 5% of the leader's probability), so the cut adapts to how confident the model is (Nguyen et al. 2024, arXiv 2407.01082). Many local runtimes offer it, and some enable it by default.

    Temperature in numbers. Take three tokens with logits [2, 1, 0]. Divide by T, then apply softmax:

    TemperatureLogits ÷ TProbabilities
    T = 0.5[4, 2, 0][0.867, 0.117, 0.016]
    T = 1[2, 1, 0][0.665, 0.245, 0.090]
    T = 2[1, 0.5, 0][0.506, 0.307, 0.186]

    The ranking never changes, so greedy decoding picks the same token at every temperature. What changes is how often sampling picks the others: the third token goes from about 1 draw in 60 at T = 0.5 to about 1 in 5 at T = 2.

    Heads up

    Decoding does not change the model's parameters — it only changes how you sample from a fixed distribution. For evaluation you usually want greedy (deterministic) decoding so results are reproducible (mostly: GPU kernels and batch composition can still change the odd token between runs); for creative generation you raise temperature/top-p.

    Greedy decoding on a small model can get stuck repeating a phrase. The usual patch is a repetition penalty, a decoding knob that lowers the scores of tokens already in the sequence. In the common Hugging Face implementation that sequence includes your prompt, so the penalty also pushes the model away from copying the input, which is exactly what extraction, classification and question answering over a passage need to do. Keep it at 1.0 (off) for those tasks, use it only for open-ended generation, and check the result on your evaluation set. Also check the model's own generation_config.json, which can switch a penalty on silently. BrewSLM's evaluations pin it to 1.0 by default for this reason. Decoding controls in Track 1 covers the details.

    What this means for fine-tuning

    Fine-tuning, the subject of the rest of this course, works on exactly this machine. SFT shows the model examples of the inputs you care about and the outputs you want, and runs the same next-token training so that, for your task, the distribution it produces favors the responses you want. You are not bolting on a new ability; you are reshaping the next-token probabilities a base model already has.

    That's the full Track-0 mechanism. The next lessons zoom out: the ways to steer a model (prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, pretraining), why small models are worth the effort, what a project looks like, and how to choose a starting model.

    Recap

    • The LM head turns the last layer into one logit per vocabulary token, and softmax turns logits into next-token probabilities.
    • Training minimises cross-entropy, −ln p of the true next token in nats, at every position of every example at once.
    • Generation repeats "predict, choose, append"; decoding settings (greedy, temperature, top-k, top-p, min-p, repetition penalty) change the choice, not the model.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    A model gives the next token the logits [3, 1, 0, −1] for the tokens "yes", "no", "maybe", "unsure". (1) What are the probabilities at T = 1? (2) With top-p = 0.9, which tokens can be sampled? (3) If the true next token was "no", what is the loss in nats? Use a calculator or python -c "import math; ...".

    Show answer

    (1) e3, e1, e0, e−1 = 20.09, 2.72, 1.00, 0.37; they sum to 24.17, so the probabilities are about [0.831, 0.112, 0.041, 0.015]. (2) Sort and add: 0.831 is below 0.9, 0.831 + 0.112 = 0.943 reaches it, so only "yes" and "no" stay (renormalised to about 0.88 and 0.12). (3) −ln 0.112 ≈ 2.19 nats. Had the answer been "yes", the loss would be −ln 0.831 ≈ 0.19 nats.

    Key terms

    LM head
    The final layer producing a score (logit) for every vocabulary token.
    Logits
    Raw, unnormalized scores for each possible next token.
    Softmax
    Turns logits into a probability distribution that sums to 1.
    Cross-entropy
    The training loss; small when the true next token was given high probability.
    Autoregressive generation
    Producing text by repeatedly predicting and appending the next token.
    Greedy / sampling
    Take the most likely token, or randomly draw according to probabilities.
    Temperature / top-p
    Decoding knobs that flatten/sharpen the distribution and trim the unlikely tail.
    Top-k / min-p
    Tail-trimming rules: keep the k most likely tokens, or keep tokens at least a set fraction as likely as the top one.
    Nats
    The unit of cross-entropy computed with the natural log; −ln p for the true token.
